property_summary: For any caller and any msg.value, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) the fallback call iff msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant instead accepts when msg.value == 5 ether, so there exist inputs where the reference accepts but the mutant rejects (and vice versa).

For every call to C's fallback with any sender and any timestamp/block, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) exactly when msg.value == 10 ether; therefore for all inputs where msg.value == 10 ether the call succeeds and leaves address(c).balance increased by that amount — the mutant changes the accepted value to 5 ether and will reject some inputs (e.g. msg.value == 10 ether) that the reference accepts.

For any caller and any sent value, C's fallback accepts (does not revert) exactly when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant changes that acceptance to msg.value == 5 ether, so there exist fuzzed msg.value inputs where the reference accepts but the mutant rejects (or vice versa).

For every call to C.fallback, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) exactly when msg.value == 10 ether; the mutant instead accepts when msg.value == 5 ether, so there exist fuzzed msg.value inputs where the reference accepts and the mutant reverts (or vice versa).

For every call to C's fallback, the reference contract accepts (does not revert) iff msg.value == 10 ether, so for any fuzzed msg.value the reference will succeed exactly on 10 ether while the mutant that requires 5 ether will reject those 10 ether calls (and thus the predicate 'fallback-call-succeeds when msg.value == 10 ether' holds for the reference but is violated by the mutant).

For every call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether, C always updates pastBlockTime to a strictly greater block.timestamp than its previous value (i.e., block.timestamp increases when pastBlockTime is updated); the mutant that removes the require(block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) can allow pastBlockTime to be set to a non-greater (equal) timestamp for some inputs (same timestamp), violating this rule.

After any successful fallback call that sends exactly 10 ether, the contract's public pastBlockTime strictly increases (new value > previous value); the mutant can set pastBlockTime to the same timestamp (or not strictly greater) when two calls occur within the same block/time, violating this rule.

For any caller and block timestamp, calling fallback with exactly 10 ether never makes the contract send its entire balance to a callee whose fallback reverts (the reference first requires time to advance before updating pastBlockTime so a malicious callee that reverts cannot be paid), but the mutant that removes the timestamp check can update pastBlockTime and then attempt a transfer which will revert for some inputs causing observable difference.

For every call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether, the reference contract only ever forwards its entire balance (via transfer) when the call occurs in a strictly later timestamp than the previously recorded pastBlockTime; the mutant that removes the timestamp check can sometimes allow a transfer to happen even when the timestamp did not advance, causing the transfer (and thus address(c).balance == 0) for some fuzzed block timestamp/number inputs.

Reference C never allows its pastBlockTime to be updated when block.timestamp is less-than-or-equal to the previously recorded pastBlockTime (i.e., fallback only updates pastBlockTime if time strictly advances); the mutant (which removed the timestamp check) can update pastBlockTime even when timestamp does not increase, so for some fuzzed sequences the getter pastBlockTime will be set to a non-greater value violating that rule.

After any successful payable call to fallback with exactly 10 ether and a strictly increasing block.timestamp, the contract's public getter pastBlockTime must equal the current block.timestamp; the mutant that stores block.number instead breaks this when block.timestamp != block.number (which occurs for many inputs).

When fallback pays out (every 15th block) the reference contract always sends the balance to msg.sender (the direct caller) whereas the mutant sends it to tx.origin — thus for some caller contexts (an intermediate contract calling C) the reference will credit the intermediate contract (msg.sender) while the mutant credits the original EOA (tx.origin), changing C's balance after the call; the rule: after any fallback invocation by a contract-caller, if block.number % 15 == 0 then C.balance == 0 (reference), but the mutant can leave C.balance != 0 when the intermediate contract does not receive funds (since funds went to tx.origin).

For any call to C.fallback made by a contract (not an EOA) that sends the required 10 ether at a block where block.number % 15 == 0, the reference contract always forwards its full balance to msg.sender (so C.balance == 0 after the call); the mutant forwards to tx.origin and can leave C.balance != 0 for some inputs (a contract caller), which violates this rule.

For any call to C.fallback made by a contract caller that sends exactly 10 ether at a block where block.number % 15 == 0, the reference contract always forwards its full balance to the immediate caller (so address(c).balance == 0 after the call); the mutant forwarding to tx.origin can leave address(c).balance != 0 for some inputs (contract caller vs EOA origin), violating this rule.

For any call to C.fallback by an intermediate contract that sends exactly 10 ether at a block where block.number % 15 == 0, the reference always results in address(c).balance == 0 (because it transfers the contract balance to msg.sender), whereas the mutant that pays tx.origin can leave address(c).balance != 0 for some choices of the intermediate caller and tx.origin.

For any call to C.fallback made by a contract (intermediate caller) that sends exactly 10 ether at a block where block.number % 15 == 0, the correct contract always results in address(c).balance == 0 (it transfers its balance to msg.sender), whereas the mutant sending to tx.origin can leave address(c).balance != 0 when tx.origin != msg.sender (i.e., when the immediate caller is a contract and the ultimate origin is an EOA).

After any successful call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from any EOA with block.timestamp strictly greater than previous pastBlockTime, the contract's public pastBlockTime must equal the current block.timestamp (the mutant sometimes stores double that value), and the mutant violates this for inputs where the call succeeds.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from any caller when block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp (getter returns block.timestamp) after the call; the mutant sometimes stores a doubled value and thus violates this rule for some inputs.

After any successful fallback call that sends exactly 10 ether and where block.timestamp is strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp (observable via the public getter), while the mutant that omits the assignment leaves pastBlockTime unchanged for some inputs (so the stored value differs).

After any successful fallback call (with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp strictly greater than pastBlockTime), the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp; the mutant that omits the assignment fails to update pastBlockTime for some inputs, so pastBlockTime after the call can remain unchanged.

For any caller and any valid timestamp/chain state where block.timestamp increases, after a successful fallback call the contract's pastBlockTime is updated to the current block.timestamp in the reference; the mutant that delays the assignment can leave pastBlockTime unchanged when a transfer happens (so the mutant can differ), allowing a transfer to occur using the old pastBlockTime while the reference always updates pastBlockTime to the current timestamp on every successful fallback.

For any successful payable fallback call with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp; the mutant that moves the assignment after a conditional transfer can fail to update pastBlockTime when a transfer occurs (so pastBlockTime may remain old).

For any successful payable call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference C always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp after the call; the mutant can perform a transfer during fallback that causes pastBlockTime to remain unchanged (because assignment was moved after the transfer), so there exist inputs (a call occurring on a block where block.number % 15 == 0 and to a recipient whose receive/ fallback forcibly reverts the transfer) that make the mutant leave pastBlockTime unchanged while the reference still updates it.

For any successful payable fallback call with msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to block.timestamp; the mutant can have a failing transfer to the caller (on blocks where block.number % 15 == 0) that causes pastBlockTime to remain unchanged, so there exist inputs (a call on such a block to a reverting recipient) that make the mutant violate this invariant.

For any admissible fallback call sending exactly 10 ether and with block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference C always updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp; the mutant can fail to update pastBlockTime when a conditional transfer occurs (on blocks where block.number % 15 == 0) and that transfer to the caller reverts, so pastBlockTime may remain old.
